newsitem.title: UK: Malaysian in match-rigging case asked to pump stars.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian in match-rigging case asked to pump stars.

text.p: A Malaysian businessman accused of helping to rig English soccer matches told a court on Monday he had been asked to pump players for inside information but said he did not think it was illegal.

Heng Suan Lim was asked to explain a 1987 letter, seized by police after his arrest, in which family friend Ong Chi Kyu asked for the information to help him make money by betting in Malaysia on the results of English games.
Soccer stars Bruce Grobbelaar, John Fashanu and Hans Segers face charges along with Lim of conspiring to fix English premier league matches. They deny the charges.
They are accused of conspiring together to give and accept gifts of money as inducements to influence the outcome of soccer matches improperly or as rewards for having done so.
If convicted, they could face sentences of up to seven years in jail and unlimited fines.

The letter, read out in court by Lim's lawyer, Jerome Lynch, said: "You must mix with some teams and get to know the players. Don't make any promises. Just make friends and talk about soccer. You must be careful."
"Did you understand this to be an invitation to do something illegal?" asked Lynch.
"Absolutely not," replied Lim, 31, making his first appearance in the dock at the start of the trial's fourth week.

"What he wanted me to do was to mix with players to get inside information. The players would know about the line-ups, the state of health of the team... whether a certain player was very important to the team," Lim said.
The stocky businessman, who moved to England to study accountancy in 1986, said he had made no effort to contact players in 1987 or in 1988.
Malaysia's Chinese community liked to bet unofficially on the results of English soccer matches, said Lim who sent Kyu details of the odds which English bookmakers were offering on certain matches.

Asked to explain why Kyu had mentioned in an earlier letter that the two men could soon be making money, Lim said:"I think he could have got this information from newspapers in Malaysia but later than (it was available) in England. It would certainly have been an advantage to get it from me."
Lim told the court he had become obsessed with soccer while in a Kuala Lumpur orphanage from the ages of 10 to 16 and had eventually played for the Malaysian Under-18's national side.
